name: Vitess
summary: A proxy layer, born at YouTube, that shards MySQL across many servers while the app still sees one database.
intro: Vitess puts a layer of Go processes between your app and many ordinary MySQL servers. The app connects to VTGate with any MySQL driver. VTGate parses each query, looks up the VSchema, which says how each table is sharded, and sends the query to the right shards, merging results when it has to ask several. A keyspace is a logical database; in a sharded keyspace a vindex function such as `xxhash` turns each row’s sharding key into a keyspace ID, and each shard owns a range of IDs (`-80`, `80-`). Next to every MySQL instance runs a VTTablet that pools connections, rewrites or kills harmful queries, and manages replication and backups. Cluster state lives in a topology service (etcd by default, ZooKeeper or Consul), which is not on the query path, so queries keep flowing if it is briefly down.

Operations are workflows. `MoveTables` and `Reshard` copy data to new keyspaces or shards with VReplication, verify it with `VDiff`, then switch reads and writes over with seconds of read-only time. VTOrc watches every shard and runs an emergency reparent when a primary dies; semi-sync replication is recommended so failover loses no data. Vitess supports MySQL and Percona Server 8.0 and 8.4; v24 is the last release with 8.0. It is free under Apache 2.0, a graduated CNCF project, runs on Kubernetes through an open-source operator, and is sold as a managed service by PlanetScale, founded by its co-creators.
strengths: Horizontal sharding of MySQL without sharding code in the app, and online resharding as data grows
Lightweight client connections multiplexed onto small MySQL pools, so thousands of connections are cheap
Automated failover with VTOrc, online schema changes, backups to S3, GCS or Ceph, and cell-aware multi-region layouts
Proven at scale: it served all of YouTube’s database traffic for years, and Slack, Square, GitHub and JD.com adopted it
Vendor-neutral governance under the CNCF since 2018, with PlanetScale as a managed option
limits: Not all of MySQL: `CALL` works only on an unsharded keyspace or a targeted shard, `CREATE PROCEDURE` must go to MySQL directly, views in sharded keyspaces are experimental and read-only, and temporary tables work only unsharded
Cross-shard reads may be inconsistent with each other and run at READ COMMITTED; atomic cross-shard writes need 2PC mode, which costs about 50% more per write
Sharded tables lose `auto_increment` to Vitess sequences, and a poor sharding key turns common queries into expensive scatter queries
Many moving parts to run: VTGate, VTTablet per MySQL, vtctld, VTOrc and a topology cluster; prebuilt binaries are fully supported only on Ubuntu
MySQL and Percona only: MariaDB can be imported but not run, and MySQL 8.0 users must move to 8.4 after v24

sections.title: The parts of a Vitess cluster
sections.intro: Each is a separate process; a small test cluster runs them all on one machine, production spreads them across hosts or pods.

items.name: VTGate
items.text: Speaks the MySQL protocol (and gRPC) to apps, plans queries against the VSchema and routes them to shards. Run as many as you need behind a load balancer.

items.name: VTTablet
items.text: Sits beside each `mysqld`: connection pooling, query rules and limits, replication management, backups and the VReplication streams behind `MoveTables` and `Reshard`.

items.name: Topology service
items.text: A global store for keyspaces, shards and each shard’s primary, plus a local one per cell for its tablets. Used for discovery and locks, not for serving queries.

items.name: VTOrc
items.text: A fork of Orchestrator that elects a primary for new shards, runs an emergency reparent when one dies, and fixes replication settings, following the keyspace’s durability policy.

items.name: vtctld and vtctldclient
items.text: The admin server and CLI for schema and VSchema changes, workflows and reparenting.

items.name: VTAdmin
items.text: A web UI (`vtadmin-web`) and API (`vtadmin-api`) for looking after clusters.

sections.title: What changes when you shard MySQL with Vitess
sections.intro: Within one shard, a query behaves as in MySQL. These are the differences once a keyspace has several shards.

rows.label: Transactions
values: REPEATABLE READ within a shard; READ COMMITTED across shards, atomic only in 2PC mode

rows.label: `auto_increment`
values: Replaced by sequences: a single-row table in an unsharded keyspace hands out IDs in cached chunks

rows.label: Stored procedures
values: `CALL` only on a targeted shard, `IN` parameters only, no result sets

rows.label: Views
values: Experimental, read-only, all tables in one keyspace

rows.label: Joins and aggregates
values: Mostly supported; VTGate merges results, and joins on the sharding key stay on one shard

rows.label: Schema changes
values: Managed online DDL across all shards, or plain DDL

story: In 2010 YouTube’s MySQL database was close to running out of capacity at peak. Read replicas helped until writes outgrew a single primary, and then the application itself had to know which shard held each row. Vitess, created that year, moved that logic out of the app into a proxy between the app and MySQL, which also handles failover, connection pooling and protection from bad queries.

At YouTube it ran on Borg, Google’s cluster manager, and served all database traffic for more than five years while YouTube’s user base grew more than 50-fold. It was also released as open source. Version 2.0 reached general availability in 2016. In February 2018 the CNCF accepted Vitess as an incubating project, the same year its co-creators founded PlanetScale to sell it as a service, and in November 2019 it became the eighth CNCF project to graduate.
Vitess showed that MySQL could be scaled out without changing databases, and companies such as Slack, Square and GitHub adopted it.

choices.choice: A proxy instead of sharding logic in the app
choices.why: YouTube’s code had to pick a shard before every query. Moving routing into VTGate let the app see one database while the data spread over many MySQL servers.
Each shard is still a MySQL primary with replicas, managed by a VTTablet beside it, so the storage engine, replication and tooling stay ones teams already trust.
Vitess recommends about 250 GB per MySQL server: smaller instances replicate, back up and restore faster, and an outage affects less data.
At YouTube it ran on Borg, so it was designed for processes that move between machines; the same design fits Kubernetes.

timeline.text: Created at YouTube to scale its MySQL databases
Accepted by the CNCF on 5 February; PlanetScale founded
Graduates from the CNCF on 5 November, the eighth project to do so
